school.m: People gathered to debate in their free time, when they didn't have to work, and that grew into school.

bread.h: Korean ppang (bread) is a Portuguese word
bread.m: Portuguese traders brought pão to Japan in the 1500s, and from Japan the word made its way to Korea.

mama.h: Korean eomma and Chinese mama aren't related
mama.m: ‘Ma’ is the first sound a baby can make, so unrelated languages arrived at the same answer independently.

vodka.m: Russian voda (water) plus a suffix meaning small. Voda shares a root with English water.

tea.h: Tea and Korean cha come from one Chinese character
tea.m: Both are 茶. The te pronunciation traveled by sea to Europe, while cha spread overland to Korea and Russia.

coffee.h: Coffee is the same word in almost every language
coffee.m: Arabic qahwa spread around the world by way of Turkish and Italian.

gabae.m: It's the Korean reading of 珈琲, the Chinese characters chosen to spell out the sound of coffee.

mother.h: Mother and madre were once the same word
mother.m: They're siblings, all branching off from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.

father.h: Father has an f, padre a p. Why?
father.m: In the Germanic languages, p shifted to f across the board. It's Grimm's law, worked out by Jacob Grimm of the Brothers Grimm.

foot.h: Foot and pedal split from the same word
foot.m: Thanks to Grimm's law, only Germanic got the f. Latin kept the p, which gave us pedal and pedestrian.

heart.h: Heart and courage share a root
heart.m: Latin cor (heart) gave French cœur and English courage. In Germanic, k shifted to h, giving heart.

focus.m: The hearth was the center of the home. The French and Spanish words for fire, feu and fuego, come from it too.

nocturne.m: Latin nox (night) gave us both nocturnal and nocturne.

namae.h: Japanese namae looks like name by pure chance
namae.m: It comes from native Japanese na (name), with no link to European languages. Name and French nom, though, really are relatives.

novel.m: Latin novus (new) gave us novel, and also nova, a ‘new star’.

disaster.m: Dis (bad) plus astro (star). It meant misfortune caused by an unlucky position of the stars.

month.m: Months were measured by the moon's cycle. Same idea as the Chinese character 月, which means both moon and month.

soleil.m: It comes from Latin sol (sun) plus a suffix meaning small.

taiyang.m: That's yang as in yin and yang. The moon is taeeum (太陰), ‘greatest yin’, and in Korean the lunar calendar is named after it.

dandelion.m: From French dent de lion, named for its leaves, which are jagged like the teeth of a saw.

sam.h: Sam, san and sān (three) are the same word
sam.m: All three split off from Middle Chinese sam. The native Korean word for three, set, comes from a different line.

salad.m: Latin sal (salt) gave us not just salad but sauce and even sausage.

salary.h: Paid in salt? That salary story is ‘shaky’
salary.m: Salary is linked to salt, but there's little record of Roman soldiers actually being paid in salt.

galaxy.m: Greek gala means milk. The Milky Way looked like a trail of spilled milk, hence the name.

casino.m: It's Italian casa (house) plus a suffix meaning small.

mansion.h: French maison (house) and mansion are siblings
mansion.m: Both come from Latin mansio, a place to stay.

dog.h: The origin of dog is still a mystery
dog.m: German Hund and French chien share a root, but where dog and Spanish perro came from remains unknown.

maharaja.m: Latin rex and Sanskrit raja share a root, and maha means great.

king.h: King probably goes back to kin
king.m: The leading theory is that a king was the head of the kin, the family clan. It isn't settled, though.

museum.m: Music, too, comes from a Greek word meaning the art of the Muses.

pomegranate.m: Latin pomum originally meant just fruit. That's why the French word for apple is pomme.

manzana.h: Spanish manzana (apple) is named after a Roman
manzana.m: It comes from an apple variety named after a Roman called Matius.

foreign.m: It comes from Latin foras (outside the door), which shares a root with door.

gasu.h: Korean gasu (歌手, singer) is a ‘singing hand’
gasu.m: 歌 is song, and 手 is hand in the sense of a skilled person, like a deckhand. Korean, Chinese and Japanese all share this word.

manual.h: Manual and manicure both come from ‘hand’
manual.m: Latin manus (hand) also gave us manuscript, something written by hand.

tide.m: The German word for time is Zeit, which shares a root with tide.

mermaid.m: English says sea, but an older root for it survives in mermaid.

nevada.m: In Spanish, snow is nieve and snow-covered is nevada.

library.m: Latin liber originally meant the inner bark of a tree, because that's what people wrote on.

book.h: One theory says book comes from the beech tree
book.m: The idea is that it comes from letters carved into beech-wood boards.

eau.h: French eau is aqua, worn all the way down
eau.m: The sounds kept wearing away in French until it became eau, which is pronounced simply ‘oh’.

milk.m: It's written 牛乳, cow plus milk. Korean, Chinese and Japanese all use the character 牛 for cow.

snow.h: Snow and French neige share a root
snow.m: On the way into Latin the initial s fell off, giving nix, which became French neige and Spanish nieve.

bd-pupil.m: It's from the tiny image of yourself reflected in someone else's eye. Korean calls that image nunbucheo.

bd-daisy.m: From Old English dæges eage. The petals open at dawn and close at dusk.

bd-ear-corn.h: Your ear and an ear of corn are unrelated
bd-ear-corn.m: The body part is kin to German Ohr and Latin auris; the grain ear, to German Ähre. Only in English did they end up sounding alike, by chance.

bd-self-nose.h: 自 (self) was originally a picture of a ‘nose’
bd-self-nose.m: In oracle bone script, 自 is shaped like a nose. Once 自 came to mean self, a separate character, 鼻, was created for nose.

bd-gobbul.why: Native Korean word history: the 뿔 in 고뿔 was 불 (fire), from Middle Korean 곳블 (코+ㅅ+블). Only works if you read Hangul.

bd-rhino.m: Greek rhis (nose) plus keras (horn). Korean koppulso was built the same way: nose + horn + cow.

bd-mouth.h: Mouth is missing an n it should have
bd-mouth.m: In Old English, n vanished before th, s and f. Five vs. German fünf and us vs. uns are the same story.

bd-stomach.m: Greek stomachos, from stoma (mouth), originally meant the throat. Only later did it come to mean the stomach.

bd-lingua.h: Tongue and Latin lingua were once the same word
bd-lingua.m: The leading theory: Old Latin dingua became lingua, influenced by lingere (to lick). Language comes from it too.

bd-ipsul.why: Native Korean word history: 입술 and 눈시울 share 시울 (curved edge), via Middle Korean 입시울. Only works in Hangul.

bd-eolgul.m: In the 15th century, eolgul meant form or appearance; by the 17th it had narrowed to the face. Latin facies, too, first meant appearance.

bd-lose-face.h: Lose face is a translation from Chinese
bd-lose-face.m: It's English for Chinese 丢脸 (to lose face), on record since 1835.

bd-tete.m: Latin testa was an earthenware pot or a shell. It's uncertain whether the head was jokingly called a jar or the skull was called a shell.

bd-mari.h: The Korean counter for animals, mari, meant ‘head’
bd-mari.m: In Middle Korean, mari meant head. Many languages count animals by the head, like Japanese 一頭 or 50 head of cattle.

bd-meorikarak.why: Korean sound change: the leftover ㅎ in 머리카락, 살코기, 안팎. Only works if you read Hangul.

bd-shampoo.m: From Hindi champo (press!). It meant massaging the body, then around 1860 came to mean washing the hair.

bd-epaule.m: Latin spatula came to mean the broad, flat shoulder blade. In Spanish it became espalda, the back.

bd-bra.m: French bras (arm) gave a word for an arm guard, which shifted to a child's top and then to underwear.

bd-cubit.h: The cubit, as in Noah's ark, means ‘elbow’
bd-cubit.m: From Latin cubitum (elbow). One cubit is the length from elbow to fingertip, roughly half a meter.

bd-digit.m: Counting on fingers turned digit into a word for the numerals 0–9. Process something as numbers, and it's digital.

bd-garak.why: Depends on Korean spelling: 손가락/젓가락 share the native word 가락.

bd-knee.h: The k in knee used to be pronounced
bd-knee.m: English once pronounced the k, just like German. It weakened over about 100 years and disappeared around 1750, surviving only in the spelling.

bd-leg-skin.h: Leg and skin are words the Vikings left behind
bd-leg-skin.m: Both came in from Old Norse. Before that, English called a leg a shank and skin hide.

bd-bein.m: The meaning widened from bone to the whole leg. Elfenbein, ivory, means ‘elephant bone’.

bd-gips.h: Korean gipseu (a cast) is German for ‘plaster’
bd-gips.m: It seems to have come from German Gips (plaster) by way of Japanese gipusu.

bd-bless.m: From Germanic *blodison, to mark with blood: a rite of sprinkling an altar with blood to make it holy.

bd-brainwash.h: Brainwashing is translated straight from Chinese
bd-brainwash.m: It's said to be a literal rendering of Chinese 洗脑 (wash the brain), from around 1950. Korean senoe uses the same characters.

bd-shinkei.m: In Kaitai Shinsho, Sugita Genpaku rendered Dutch zenuw as 神經: the meridian (經脈) of the vital spirit (神氣).

bd-film.m: Old English filmen was a thin membrane or skin. Around 1845 it came to name the thin coating on photographic plates.

bd-muscle.m: A rippling muscle looked like a mouse under the skin. Mussel comes from the same Latin musculus.

bd-ventriloquism.m: It joins Latin venter (belly) and loqui (to speak). Korean bokhwasul (腹話術) means the same.

bd-spirit.m: From Latin spirare (to breathe). Likewise expire, to breathe out, came to mean both to die and to run out.

bd-doctor.m: From Latin docere (to teach). Once a title for scholars, it came to mean a physician around 1400.

bd-yi.h: 醫, the character for doctor, contains ‘liquor’
bd-yi.m: The 酉 at the bottom is a liquor jar. The Shuowen Jiezi explains it as ‘because illness is cured with liquor’.

bd-mes.m: Dutch mes came via Japanese mesu. In the Netherlands even a kitchen knife is simply a mes.

bd-vaccine.m: It comes from Jenner using cowpox, a disease of cows, to prevent smallpox. Pasteur extended the name to vaccines for other diseases.

bd-ringer.h: Korean ringgeo (IV drip) is ‘a person's name’
bd-ringer.m: It's named for the solution British doctor Sydney Ringer made in the 1880s for experiments on frog hearts.

bd-cemetery.m: It's Greek for a place to sleep. Early Christians saw death as sleep and gave the name to burial grounds.

bd-nightmare.h: The mare in nightmare isn't a horse
bd-nightmare.m: A mare was a demon that pressed down on sleepers. It only sounds like mare, the female horse; they're unrelated.

bd-morphine.h: Morphine is named after the god of dreams
bd-morphine.m: Because it brings on sleep, German pharmacist Sertürner named it after Morpheus, the god of dreams.

bd-gamgi.h: Gamgi (感氣, a cold) is Korea's own coinage
bd-gamgi.m: It's a Korean-made word in Chinese characters, seen from the late 18th century on. China says 感冒 and Japan says 風邪.

bd-korper.h: German Körper (body) is a borrowed word
bd-korper.m: It was borrowed from Latin corpus (body) in the 13th century. The old word for body, lîch, survives only in Leiche (corpse).

bd-gesund.h: Sound and Gesundheit share a root
bd-gesund.m: Sound meaning healthy is unrelated to sound the noise, but kin to German gesund. Gesundheit! after a sneeze means ‘health!’

bd-wisaeng.h: Korean wisaeng (hygiene) is borrowed from Zhuangzi
bd-wisaeng.m: In the early Meiji era, Nagayo Sensai translated German Hygiene as 衛生, ‘guarding life’, a term taken from Zhuangzi.

pp-hermano.h: Frère and hermano (brother) have different roots
pp-hermano.m: Hermano keeps only germanus from Latin frater germanus (full brother). The usual view is that it's unrelated to the name of the Germans.

pp-cousin.h: Cousin has a ‘sister’ hiding inside it
pp-cousin.m: Latin consobrinus first meant a child of your mother's sister, and soror (sister) is tucked inside it.

pp-sohn.h: Son and sun, Sohn and Sonne: pure coincidence
pp-sohn.m: Son comes from a root meaning to give birth; sun, from an unrelated root for the sun. In English and German alike, the match is an accident.

pp-daughter.h: Latin lost its own version of daughter
pp-daughter.m: The word died out in Latin, which used filia, the feminine of filius (son), instead. That became Spanish hija.

pp-niang.h: 娘 means mom in China and daughter in Japan
pp-niang.m: Chinese 娘 can mean young lady or mother. In Japanese it means daughter, and Korean keeps it in nangja (娘子).

pp-kind.h: German Kind and English child aren't related
pp-kind.m: Kind comes from a root meaning to give birth, which makes it kin to gene. Child shares a root with a Gothic word for womb.

pp-kodomo.h: Japanese kodomo and tomodachi were once plurals
pp-kodomo.m: The -domo and -tachi are plural endings. Now they're used for just one person, so another plural gets stacked on, as in kodomotachi.

pp-infant.h: Infant literally means ‘one who can't speak’
pp-infant.m: Latin in (not) plus fans (speaking). Infante, once meaning a youth, also gave us infantry, the foot soldiers.

pp-akachan.m: Newborn skin has a reddish tint. The Sino-Korean word jeokja (赤子) also means a newborn baby.

pp-fiend.h: Friend and fiend were a pair of opposites
pp-fiend.m: In Old English they meant one who loves and one who hates. German Feind still means enemy.

pp-free.h: Free and friend share a root
pp-free.m: Both come from a root meaning to love. The leading theory: the free were the beloved members of the household, as opposed to slaves.

pp-enemy.m: Latin in (not) plus amicus (friend), in the same family as French ami and Spanish amigo.

pp-guest.h: Guest and hostile share a root
pp-guest.m: The root meant stranger. A stranger could be a guest or an enemy, and Latin hostis came to mean enemy.

pp-werewolf.m: Old English wer (man) shares a root with Latin vir. Virtue, too, originally meant manliness.

pp-guy.h: Guy was originally one man's name
pp-guy.m: Guy Fawkes, who plotted to blow up Parliament in 1605. Effigies of him, called guys, made guy mean man.

pp-woman.m: Old English wīfmann = wīf (female) + mann (person). Man then meant anyone, male or female, and wife just meant “woman.”

pp-persona.m: Latin persona was the mask an actor wore. The mask came to mean the role, and the role came to mean a person.

pp-ningen.h: 人間 (human) first meant ‘the world of people’
pp-ningen.m: Chinese 人间 still means “the human world.” In Korean and Japanese, it came to mean the people who live in that world.

pp-husband.h: Husband originally meant ‘master of the house’
pp-husband.m: Old Norse hús (house) + bóndi (dweller). It only came to mean “married man” in the late 13th century.

pp-zhangfu.h: 丈夫: husband in China, ‘sturdy’ in Japan
pp-zhangfu.m: It first meant “a grown man.” Japanese 大丈夫 (it's okay) went from “a fine man” through “sturdy, reliable” to get there.

pp-anae.why: Depends on Korean: native vs Sino-Korean words for husband/wife (남편/男便, 아내/안해, 여편네).

pp-manura.why: History of a native Korean word (마노라 → 마누라) and its drop in register; strip is all Korean.

pp-family.m: Latin famulus meant “servant,” and familia was all the servants in a household. Only later did it include relatives.

pp-neighbor.h: Neighbor and German Bauer share a root
pp-neighbor.m: Neigh- means “near” and -bor means “dweller.” That -bor shares a root with German Bauer (farmer).

pp-sensei.m: It literally means “born first.” In Chinese it's a polite title for men and also “husband”; in Korea and Japan it mostly means “teacher.”

pp-student.m: Latin studere meant “to be eager, to strive.” A person keen on something became a student.

pp-sarang.h: Korean saranghada (to love) once meant ‘to think’
pp-sarang.m: In Middle Korean, saranghada mostly meant “to think” (思). By the early modern era, only the “love” (愛) sense was left.

pp-airen.h: 愛人: spouse in China, ‘lover on the side’ in Japan
pp-airen.m: In mainland China it means a husband or wife; in Japan, the partner in an affair. Korean aein just means a sweetheart.

pp-bonheur.m: Its heur comes from Latin augurium (omen) and means “luck.” It just sounds like heure (hour); the two are unrelated.

pp-sad.m: It went from “sated, had enough” to “heavy, weary,” and then to “sorrowful.” German satt still means “full.”

pp-fear.m: Old English fǣr meant “sudden danger, calamity.” It shares a root with German Gefahr (danger).

pp-cry.m: From Latin quiritare (to scream). The “shed tears” sense came later and pushed aside the older word, weep.

pp-hello.h: Hello took off thanks to the telephone
pp-hello.m: In 1877 Edison recommended it as a phone greeting, and it spread widely. Bell pushed for ahoy, but hello won.

pp-happy.m: From hap (chance, luck), which also gave us happen and perhaps. German Glück means both “luck” and “happiness.”

pp-goodbye.h: Goodbye was once ‘God be with you’
pp-goodbye.m: “God be with ye” got shortened, and God turned into good, influenced by “good day.” Adieu and adiós also mean “to God.”

pp-ciao.m: It was a Venetian dialect greeting: “(I am) your servant.” Servus, a greeting in Austria, is also Latin for “servant.”

pp-sayonara.h: Sayonara literally means ‘if that's the case’
pp-sayonara.m: It's short for 左様ならば, “if that is so.” A sign-off like “well then, I'll be off” became the word for goodbye.

pp-thank.h: Thank and think share a root
pp-thank.m: Both come from a Germanic word that meant “thought” and “gratitude” at once. German has the same pair: danken and denken.

pp-merci.m: Latin merces (wages, reward) shifted to “favor, mercy” and then to “thank you.” It's also related to market.

pp-arigato.h: Arigatō originally meant ‘hard to come by’
pp-arigato.m: From 有り難い: rare and precious in this world. The idea that it comes from Portuguese obrigado is a popular myth.

pp-sorry.m: Sorry comes from sore (painful); sorrow has a different root. Sorry's spelling just drifted toward sorrow, giving it the o.

pp-mian.h: Korean mian (sorry) means ‘not yet at ease’
pp-mian.m: 未 (not) + 安 (at ease): a Sino-Korean word for when you've caused someone trouble and your own heart isn't at ease.

pp-bead.m: People counted their prayers on rosary beads. It shares a root with German Gebet (prayer) and bitte (please).

pp-lord.m: Old English hlāf (bread) + weard (keeper). One theory says lady was the “bread kneader,” but it's uncertain.

pp-companion.h: Companion means someone you ‘eat bread with’
pp-companion.m: Latin com (with) + panis (bread). Company comes from the same word.

nt-hama.h: Hippopotamus and 河馬 both mean ‘river horse’
nt-hama.m: Greek hippos (horse) + potamos (river) matches 河 (river) + 馬 (horse). German calls it Nilpferd, “Nile horse.”

nt-crocodile.m: The “pebble + worm” reading is famous, but scholars are skeptical. Herodotus said it was originally the name of a lizard.

nt-kirin.m: 麒麟 is a legendary creature. In 1414 the Ming court called its first giraffe a 麒麟 too, but in Chinese today it's the “long-necked deer.”

nt-kokkiri.m: It was gokiri in the 15th century. The usual explanation: ko (nose) + gilda (to be long).

nt-sangsang.m: A story in the Han Feizi: people who'd never seen a live elephant (象) pictured one from its bones, so 象 came to mean “image.”

nt-bear.h: Bear may have meant ‘the brown one’
nt-bear.m: The leading theory: hunters avoided the bear's real name and called it “the brown one” instead.

nt-arctic.h: Arctic comes from the word for ‘bear’
nt-arctic.m: From Greek arktos (bear), for the Great Bear constellation in the northern sky. Antarctic means “opposite the Arctic.”

nt-titmouse.h: The titmouse is a bird, not a mouse
nt-titmouse.m: Old English māse meant the titmouse. In the 16th century its spelling shifted to look like the unrelated word mouse.

nt-philip.m: Greek philos (loving) + hippos (horse). The Philippines was named after the Spanish prince who would become Philip II.

nt-marshal.m: Germanic marh (horse) + skalk (servant): a stable hand rose to the top military rank. Same root as mare.

nt-hwangso.why: Korean sound change: 한쇼 (big ox) reshaped toward 黃牛 into 황소; 황새 < 한새 likewise.

nt-cattle.h: Cattle and capital were once the same word
nt-cattle.m: Both come from Latin capitale (property), from caput (head). Cattle narrowed from property to livestock, and finally to cows.

nt-pork.h: Why does a pig become pork on the plate?
nt-pork.m: After the Norman Conquest, French porc (pig) and bœuf (ox) came into English and stuck as the names for the meat.

nt-dwaeji.m: It's thought that dot (old word for pig) + -aji (a baby-animal suffix) gave doyaji, then dwaeji. Songaji (calf) and mangaji (foal) are built the same way.

nt-mi.h: 美 (beautiful) may come from a ‘big sheep’
nt-mi.m: The Shuowen Jiezi reads it as 羊 (sheep) + 大 (big) and explains it as “tasty.” Others argue it depicts an adorned person.

nt-bird.m: In Old English, a bird was fugol (today's fowl), while bridd meant a young bird. German Vogel keeps the old word.

nt-tajo.h: In Chinese characters, ostrich is ‘camel bird’
nt-tajo.m: 駝 means camel. The Greeks called it a “camel sparrow,” which lives on in its scientific name, Struthio camelus.

nt-pisces.m: Fish is thought to share a root with Latin piscis (fish). Only in the Germanic languages did p turn into f.

nt-sakana.m: 酒 (saka, alcohol) + 菜 (na, side dish): food to go with drinks. Fish was such a common drinking snack that the word came to mean fish.

nt-tsuyu.h: Japan and China call the rainy season ‘plum rain’
nt-tsuyu.m: One theory: it's the rain that comes as plums ripen. Another: the characters were changed from 黴雨, “mold rain.”

nt-nirvana.h: Nirvana and wind share a root
nt-nirvana.m: Nirvāṇa means “blown out”: the fire of worldly passions put out. Its va (to blow) shares an Indo-European root with wind.

nt-hurricane.h: Hurricane is an Indigenous Caribbean word
nt-hurricane.m: Spaniards in the 1500s took it from an Arawakan language of the West Indies as huracán, then spread it across Europe.

nt-cloud.m: Old English clūd meant a rock or hill. Billowing clouds were likened to rocks, and by about 1300 it meant “cloud.”

nt-sky.m: The Vikings' word ský (cloud) took over from heaven as the word for the sky. In Danish, sky still means “cloud.”

nt-human.m: The leading theory: humans were “earth dwellers,” as opposed to gods. It's thought to share a root with humus (soil) and humble (low to the ground).

nt-amount.m: Old French amont (toward the mountain, upward) came to mean “to go up,” then “to add up to” a total.

nt-metdwaeji.why: History of a native Korean word: 멧 in 멧돼지/멧비둘기 is the old word 뫼 (mountain).

nt-arrive.m: River and arrive both come from Latin ripa (riverbank, shore). Arriving was a boat touching the shore.

nt-gangha.h: 江 once meant the Yangtze; 河, the Yellow River
nt-gangha.m: Both were originally the names of specific rivers. That's why southern rivers still tend to be called 江, and northern ones 河.

nt-mizuumi.m: 水 (mizu, water) + 海 (umi, sea). In effect, a “freshwater sea,” as opposed to the salty one.

nt-petroleum.h: Petroleum and 石油 both mean ‘rock oil’
nt-petroleum.m: Latin petra (rock) + oleum (oil). Chinese 石油 follows the same idea and appears as early as the Song-dynasty Dream Pool Essays.

nt-island.h: The s in island is a fake
nt-island.m: Old English īegland had no s. In the 16th century an s was added to match the unrelated isle (from Latin insula).

nt-savage.m: Latin silvaticus (of the woods), from silva (forest), came to mean “wild,” then “barbaric.” Transylvania means “beyond the forest.”

nt-kinoko.m: 木 (ki, tree) + の (no, of) + 子 (ko, child): a child that sprouts from a tree.

nt-flour.h: Flour and flower were once the same word
nt-flour.m: The finest meal was called the “flower” of the grain. The two spellings only fully split around 1830.

nt-foil.h: The foil in aluminum foil originally meant ‘leaf’
nt-foil.m: From Latin folium (leaf): thin metal was likened to a leaf. Portfolio, a case for carrying papers, shares the root.

nt-green.h: Grass, green and grow share one root
nt-green.m: All from Proto-Indo-European *ghre- (to grow). Green was simply the color of growing grass.

nt-kusa.m: Laughter is 笑い (warai). Typing its w as www looked like a field of grass, so it became 草 (kusa, grass): Japan's ㅋㅋ.

nt-insect.m: Its body is divided into segments, hence Latin insectum, “cut into.” It translates Greek entomon, as in entomology.

nt-horangi.m: It's 虎狼 (tiger and wolf) plus the suffix -i. The native Korean word is beom; the form horangi appears from the late 19th century.

nt-chameleon.m: Greek khamai (on the ground) + leōn (lion). Why a lion is unclear; one explanation is that its head crest looks like a mane.

nt-singapore.m: Sanskrit siṃha (lion) + pura (city). The Sikh surname Singh is the same “lion.”

fd-arroz.h: The ar in Spanish arroz is Arabic for ‘the’
fd-arroz.m: Spanish took Arabic ar-ruzz whole, article (al) and all. Azúcar (sugar) is likewise as-sukkar.

fd-beikoku.h: In Japanese, the US is the ‘rice country’?
fd-beikoku.m: America was written 亜米利加, and Japan shortened it to just 米 (rice). Korea and China picked 美 instead, giving 美國.

fd-meat.m: The “flesh” sense only arose around 1300. The old meaning survives in sweetmeat, a sweet treat.

fd-eyren.h: Egg once baffled people in southern England
fd-eyren.m: Egg was the Vikings' Norse word. In the south people said eyren (eggs), and there's a record of egg not being understood there.

fd-egg-on.h: The egg in egg on isn't an egg
fd-egg-on.m: It's Norse eggja (to goad, incite), from egg (blade). It's spelled like the egg you eat purely by chance.

fd-sugar.m: Sanskrit śarkarā (gravel, grains) passed through Persian and Arabic on its way to Europe.

fd-satang.h: Korean for candy is Japanese for ‘sugar’
fd-satang.m: Both are written 砂糖, literally “sand sugar.” Korean satang also once meant sugar, a trace kept in satangsusu (sugarcane).

fd-norange.h: Orange originally started with an n
fd-norange.m: The leading theory: in phrases like une narange, the n got mixed up with the article and fell off. Spanish naranja kept it.

fd-apfelsine.h: In German, an orange is a ‘Chinese apple’
fd-apfelsine.m: Dutch sinaasappel, “Chinese apple,” spread to German and Russian. Turkish portakal, meanwhile, comes from “Portugal.”

fd-basho.h: The poet Bashō's name means ‘banana tree’
fd-basho.m: A disciple planted a bashō (Japanese banana tree) by his hut, and he took the plant's name as his pen name.

fd-gamja.h: Potato and Korean gamja first meant ‘sweet potato’
fd-gamja.m: Gamja comes from gamjeo (甘藷), which first meant the sweet potato. Potato, too, comes from batata (sweet potato), a Caribbean word.

fd-kartoffel.m: Italians called the potato, dug from the ground, tartufolo (little truffle), and the name passed into German.

fd-tomatl.h: Tomato and avocado are Aztec words
fd-tomatl.m: Nahuatl tomatl and ahuacatl spread through Spanish. Chili and chocolate are Nahuatl words too.

fd-fanqie.h: In Chinese, a tomato is a ‘foreign eggplant’
fd-fanqie.m: 番 marks things brought in from abroad, and 茄 is eggplant. It's also called 西红柿, “red persimmon from the west.”

fd-cocoa.m: Cocoa is cacao, from Nahuatl, altered under the influence of coco. Coco means “grimacing face,” which the holes in the shell resemble.

fd-garlic.m: Old English gār (spear) + lēac (leek): cloves were likened to spearheads. The Lauch in German Knoblauch also means “leek.”

fd-onion.h: Onion and union are the same word
fd-onion.m: From Latin unio (oneness). It's thought to be because an onion is one layered bulb, unlike garlic, which splits into cloves.

fd-yangpa.m: 洋 marks things from the West, across the sea. Yangmal (socks) are “Western beoseon” (Korean socks), and yangcho is a “Western candle.”

fd-huchu.why: Hinges on Korean sound changes: the 후 in 후추 and 호 in 호두 are both 胡 (호초 → 후추, 호도 → 호두).

fd-vinegar.m: French vin (wine) plus aigre (sour). When wine turns sour, it becomes vinegar.

fd-biru.h: Japanese bīru (beer) is a Dutch word
fd-biru.m: It's from bier, the word Dutch traders used in the Edo period. Chinese 啤酒 pairs 啤, for the sound, with 酒 (alcohol).

fd-cheese.h: Why is fromage so different from cheese?
fd-cheese.m: Cheese, Käse and queso come from Latin caseus (cheese). Fromage comes from forma, the mold cheese was pressed into.

fd-butter.m: It's usually read as Greek bous (cow) + tyros (cheese), but another theory says it's a Scythian word reinterpreted as Greek.

fd-supper.h: Soup originally meant ‘bread soaked in broth’
fd-supper.m: Late Latin suppa was bread soaked in broth. The leading theory is that supper comes from this word, too.

fd-cookie.m: Dutch koekje, koek (cake) plus a “little” ending, came into American English. Cake, Kuchen and koek all share one root.

fd-dambae.h: Korean dambae (tobacco) is Portuguese via Japan
fd-dambae.m: It came in via Japan in the early 1600s and was called dambago before shrinking to dambae.

fd-kopf.m: In older German, kopf meant “cup,” probably from Latin cuppa, like cup. French tête likewise comes from testa, an earthenware pot.

fd-koppu.m: Goppu is Dutch kop or Portuguese copo by way of Japan; keop is English cup. They share the same root.

fd-messer.h: German Messer (knife) has meat hidden inside
fd-messer.m: Old High German mezzisahs combined “food” and “knife.” The first part shares a root with meat.

fd-hocho.m: 庖丁 originally meant “cook.” People shortened 庖丁刀, “the cook's knife,” and the name stuck to the knife.

fd-cuchara.m: Latin cochlear was reportedly a spoon for eating snails out of the shell. The cochlea in your inner ear is a “snail,” too.

fd-sutgarak.why: Korean spelling: why 숟가락 has ㄷ but 젓가락 has ㅅ (술+가락 vs 저+ㅅ+가락) only makes sense in Hangul.

fd-plata.h: Spanish plata (silver) began as ‘a flat plate’
fd-plata.m: A thin sheet of metal became silver in Spanish. The leading theory traces it to Greek platys (broad), and plato (dish) is a relative too.

fd-tisch.h: German Tisch (table) is the same word as dish
fd-tisch.m: Tisch, dish and desk all come from Latin discus (disk, platter). A word for a tray became the word for table in German.

fd-cathedral.h: A cathedral is literally ‘a church with a chair’
fd-cathedral.m: From Greek kathedra (chair). A cathedral is the church where the bishop's chair stands.

fd-mattress.m: Arabic maṭraḥ (a mat thrown down on the floor) came into Europe by way of Sicily.

fd-window.m: Old Norse vindr (wind) + auga (eye). Spanish ventana also comes from a word for wind, Latin ventus.

fd-conclave.h: Conclave means ‘a room locked with a key’
fd-conclave.m: Latin con (with) + clavis (key). Cardinals were locked in a room and couldn't come out until they had chosen a pope.

fd-shirt.h: Shirt and skirt were once ‘the same word’
fd-shirt.m: The word split into sh- in English and sk- in Norse. One theory ties both to short: a garment cut short.

fd-waishatsu.h: The wai in Korean waisyeocheu isn't Y but ‘white’
fd-waishatsu.m: Korean waisyeocheu (dress shirt) came via Japanese waishatsu, from English white shirt. The story that it's named for a Y shape is folk etymology.

fd-hojumeoni.m: Hanbok originally had no attached pockets. These add-on pouches reportedly copied the clothes of northern peoples, hence 胡, the character for “barbarian.”

fd-soap.h: Soap first shows up in writing as ‘hair dye’
fd-soap.m: The sapo Pliny first recorded was something Germanic men used to dye their hair red. The word itself is Germanic, too.

fd-candy.h: Candy and candle aren't related at all
fd-candy.m: Candle comes from Latin candela (lamp), candy from Persian qand (cane sugar).

tm-journey.h: A journey was originally ‘a day's travel’
tm-journey.m: Old French journée meant a day's work or a day's travel. Journal shares the same root, jour (day).

tm-dia.h: Day and Spanish día aren't related
tm-dia.m: Day is a sibling of German Tag, while día comes from Latin dies. The resemblance is pure coincidence.

tm-nedelya.h: The Russian word for week once meant ‘Sunday’
tm-nedelya.m: Nedelya, “the day of no work,” named Sunday before it came to mean week. Sunday was then renamed voskresenye, “resurrection.”

tm-youil.h: Korean and Japanese weekdays match Europe's
tm-youil.m: Both name the days after the sun, the moon and the five naked-eye planets, in the same order. Japanese 水曜日 and French mercredi are both Mercury's day.

tm-hour-year.h: Hour and year come from the same root
tm-hour-year.m: Greek hōra meant both season and hour. It branched off from the same year-and-season root that gave us year.

tm-nyeon.h: 年 (year) was once drawn as ‘a man carrying grain’
tm-nyeon.m: It showed a person (人) carrying grain (禾) on their back and meant harvest. Since grain is harvested once a year, it came to mean year.

tm-aujourdhui.h: The French word for today says ‘day’ twice
tm-aujourdhui.m: Hui already comes from Latin hodie (this day), so aujourd'hui is “on the day of this day.” Spanish hoy also comes from hodie.

tm-manana.h: Spanish mañana is both morning and ‘tomorrow’
tm-manana.m: “Tomorrow morning” got shortened to “tomorrow.” German Morgen also means both, and the morrow in tomorrow originally meant morning.

tm-eve.h: The eve in Christmas Eve means ‘evening’
tm-eve.m: Eve shares a root with evening and originally meant evening. German calls Christmas Eve Heiligabend, “holy evening.”

tm-noon.h: Noon was originally ‘3 in the afternoon’
tm-noon.m: From Latin nona hora, the ninth hour after sunrise, which was 3 p.m. It moved to midday between the 12th and 14th centuries.

tm-minute.h: Minute and menu come from the same root
tm-minute.m: Latin minutus means made small. A minute is a small piece cut from an hour; a menu is a list written out in small detail.

tm-second.h: A second of time is really ‘the second cut’
tm-second.m: Divide an hour by 60 and the first cut is a minute. Divide that by 60 again and the second cut is a second.

tm-myo.h: 秒 (second) first meant ‘a bristle of rice’
tm-myo.m: The old Chinese dictionary Shuowen Jiezi defines it as a rice bristle. It came to mean anything tiny, then the second: a minute split again.

tm-calendar.h: A calendar was originally ‘a debt ledger’
tm-calendar.m: Romans paid debts on the first day of each month, the kalendae. The account book that recorded them, the calendarium, became the calendar.

tm-mardi.h: French mardi and March share ‘the same god’
tm-mardi.m: Mars, the Roman war god, is also the planet Mars. His day is Tuesday (mardi, martes, 火曜日), and his month, March, opened the Roman calendar.

tm-tuesday.h: Tuesday and Zeus come from the same root
tm-tuesday.m: It's the day of the Germanic god Tīw. Tīw, Zeus and Latin deus (god) all come from a root meaning “bright sky.”

tm-wednesday.h: The silent d in Wednesday is a trace of Odin
tm-wednesday.m: It comes from Old English Wōdnesdæg, Woden's day. Woden is the Odin of Norse mythology.

tm-thursday.m: The thunder god Thor's name simply means thunder. The Roman sky god Jupiter's day (jeudi) was renamed for Thor.

tm-friday.h: Friday is the day of the goddess Frigg
tm-friday.m: The Roman day of Venus (the planet) was handed to the Germanic goddess Frigg. French vendredi and Spanish viernes still belong to Venus.

tm-pyatnitsa.h: Friday is day five in Russian, day six in Portuguese
tm-pyatnitsa.m: Russian counts from Monday and Portuguese from Sunday, so the same Friday is the fifth day (pyatnitsa) in one and the sixth (sexta-feira) in the other.

tm-saturday.h: Saturday is the only English day with a Roman god
tm-saturday.m: Tuesday through Friday swapped in Germanic gods, but Saturn stayed. One theory says there was no matching Germanic god.

tm-domingo.m: From Latin dies Dominica, the Lord's day. Dominus (master) is also the root of English dominate.

tm-september.m: It was the seventh month of the Roman calendar, which began in March. When New Year moved up to January, October (8) also slid two places.

tm-january.h: January and janitor share ‘the same door’
tm-january.m: January is the month of Janus, the two-faced god of doors and beginnings. Janitor, first a doorkeeper, comes from the same root.

tm-august.h: August has 31 days because of an emperor's ego?
tm-august.m: The story that Augustus stole a day from February arose in the Middle Ages. August already had 31 days under Caesar.

tm-lent.m: The leading theory is that it meant the time when days grow longer. Today it survives as Lent, the church season that falls in spring.

tm-verano.m: Verano comes from Latin ver (spring) and meant spring in Old Spanish. Today's word for spring is primavera, “first spring.”

tm-harvest.m: Old English hærfest was the name of the season. German Herbst still means autumn, but English handed the season's name to autumn.

tm-himalaya.h: Himalaya and hibernate share a ‘winter’ root
tm-himalaya.m: Sanskrit hima (snow) and Latin hiems (winter) share a root. Himalaya is the “abode of snow,” and to hibernate is to spend the winter.

tm-cipher.h: Zero and cipher (code) are the same word
tm-cipher.m: Both come from Arabic ṣifr (empty). Old codes swapped letters for numbers, so a word for number came to mean code.

tm-alone.m: A contraction of Old English all ana (wholly by oneself). Only also comes from a word meaning “one-like.”

tm-doubt.m: Doubt is being torn between two choices. German Zweifel (doubt) likewise comes from zwei (two).

tm-eleven.m: Count to ten and you have one left, then two left: eleven and twelve. From 13 on, it's three plus ten (teen).

tm-hundred.h: Hundred and cent were once the same word
tm-hundred.m: The ancestral k sound became h only in the Germanic languages. Latin centum gave us percent and cent.

tm-on.why: Native Korean word history: the old native numerals 온 (100) and 즈믄 (1000) lost out to Sino-Korean 백/천; nothing for a non-Korean reader to recognize.

tm-mile.m: A Roman mile was a thousand paces, counting two steps as one pace. Latin mille (thousand) became the name of the unit.

tm-million.m: Italian added -one, an ending meaning big, to mille (thousand). A million is the big number, a thousand times a thousand.

tm-krasnaya.m: In Old Russian, krasnyy meant beautiful; today pretty is krasivyy. The name is far older than communism.

tm-crimson.h: Crimson goes back to a word for ‘bug’
tm-crimson.m: The red dye came from scale insects. An Indo-Iranian word for bug reached Europe by way of Arabic.

tm-candidate.h: A candidate is literally ‘one dressed in white’
tm-candidate.m: Roman candidates for office wore dazzling white togas. The word comes from candidus (shining white), and candle is a relative.

tm-melancholy.m: People believed too much black bile made you gloomy. Melanin, which gives skin its color, also comes from melas (black).

tm-azul.h: Spanish azul (blue) began as the name of a gem
tm-azul.m: The Persian name for the blue stone lapis lazuli passed through Arabic and became azul. One theory says that name came from the place where it was mined.

tm-paranbul.h: Koreans call a green traffic light a ‘blue light’
tm-paranbul.m: Korean pureuda describes both sky and grass. Japanese ao (青) once covered green too, so a green light is aoshingō, a “blue signal.”

tm-yolk.h: Yolk and Korean noreunja both mean ‘the yellow one’
tm-yolk.m: Old English geolca (yolk) came from geolu (yellow). Korean noreunja (yolk) likewise comes from noreuda, “to be yellow.”

ct-bus.h: Bus is short for a Latin word meaning ‘for all’
ct-bus.m: It's short for voiture omnibus (carriage for all), the shared horse-drawn coaches of 1820s France.

ct-robot.m: From Czech robota (forced labor). Čapek's 1920 play spread it, but his older brother Josef came up with it.

ct-arbeit.h: Robot and German Arbeit are ‘distant cousins’
ct-arbeit.m: Arbeit (work) traveled through Japanese arubaito to become Korean alba, a part-time job. It shares an Indo-European root with Slavic rabota (work).

ct-money.h: Money is named after a goddess
ct-money.m: Rome minted its coins near the temple of the goddess Juno Moneta. Mint, where money is made, split off from the same word.

ct-fee.h: Fee goes back to a word for ‘livestock’
ct-fee.m: Livestock used to be wealth. Latin pecu (livestock) gave pecunia (money), and in Germanic the p became an f.

ct-won.h: The won, yen and yuan are ‘the same character’
ct-won.m: All three are 圓 (round), read differently in each country. It was the unit for counting round silver coins.

ct-bank.m: From Italian banca, the table where money changers laid out their coins. It shares a root with bench, so German Bank also means bench.

ct-eunhaeng.h: The 行 in 銀行 (bank) doesn't mean go but ‘shop’
ct-eunhaeng.m: Here 行 is Chinese háng, meaning a shop or line of business. A bank is a shop that deals in silver, that is, money.

ct-hotel.h: Hotel and hospital were once the same word
ct-hotel.m: Latin hospes (guest, host) gave hospitale (guesthouse), which split into hotel, hospital and hostel.

ct-restaurant.h: A restaurant was originally ‘a restoring soup’
ct-restaurant.m: From French restaurer (to restore). It started in 1760s Paris with places selling soups that restored your strength.

ct-bistro.h: Bistro is Russian for ‘quick’? That story's shaky
ct-bistro.m: The tale is that Russian soldiers in 1815 Paris shouted “Quick!” (bystro), but the word isn't recorded until 1884. Its origin is still unknown.

ct-telephone.h: The word telephone predates Bell's invention
ct-telephone.m: In 1830s France it named a signaling system that sent letters as musical notes. It's tele (far) + phone (sound).

ct-deokryulpung.h: Korea's old word for telephone was ‘deongnyulpung’
ct-deokryulpung.m: 德律風 was China's sound-for-sound spelling of telephone. The word used today, 電話, was coined in Japan.

ct-television.h: Television is half Greek and half Latin
ct-television.m: Tele (far) is Greek and vision (seeing) is Latin. German translated the idea as Fernseher, from fern (far) + sehen (to see).

ct-computer.h: Computer was once a job, not a machine
ct-computer.m: In the 1640s it meant a person who calculates; the machine sense dates from the 1890s. In Chinese a computer is diànnǎo (电脑), an “electric brain.”

ct-bug.h: Bug doesn't come from that famous moth
ct-bug.m: The moth found in a computer in 1947 was logged as the “first actual case of bug being found.” Edison was already using bug in 1878.

ct-nausea.m: From Greek naus (ship). Its relative, Latin navis (ship), gave us navy and navigate.

ct-cockpit.h: A cockpit was originally ‘a cockfighting pit’
ct-cockpit.m: It was a pit where roosters (cocks) fought. It passed to cramped quarters on warships, then became an airplane's cockpit in 1914.

ct-train.h: Train was part of a dress before it ran on rails
ct-train.m: From Latin trahere (to drag). A gown's trailing part has been a train since the 14th century; a line of cars, since the early 19th.

ct-kisha.h: In Chinese, 汽車 isn't a train but ‘a car’
ct-kisha.m: In Korean and Japanese it's a steam (汽) train, but in Chinese it's an automobile. A train in Chinese is huǒchē (火车), a “fire cart.”

ct-chauffeur.m: Early cars ran on steam. The name for the fireman who stoked the boiler passed to the driver.

ct-taxi.h: Taxi and tax come from the same root
ct-taxi.m: A taxi is a car fitted with a taximeter, a fare meter. Medieval Latin taxa (charge, fee) also gave us tax.

ct-road.m: Old English rād was a journey on horseback, and also a raid, so it's a sibling of ride and raid. The sense of a way only arose in the 1590s.

ct-metro.m: It's short for the Paris Métropolitain (metropolitan railway). In Greek, a colony's home city was its “mother city.”

ct-country.m: From Latin contra (opposite), it meant the land spread out before your eyes. It shifted to mean a region, then a nation.

ct-dutch.m: Dutch and Deutsch are one word meaning “of the people.” English narrowed Dutch to the Netherlands only in the 17th century; in Dutch, Duits means German.

ct-gage.h: Korean gage (shop) was once ‘a makeshift house’
ct-gage.m: It comes from gaga (假家), a temporary house. Places for storing goods or resting are thought to have become places of trade.

ct-boutique.h: A boutique and a pharmacy come from one word
ct-boutique.m: Greek apothēkē (storehouse) split into French boutique, Spanish bodega and German Apotheke (pharmacy).

ct-bureau.h: A bureau was originally ‘a piece of cloth’
ct-bureau.m: Burel, the coarse wool cloth that covered desks, came to mean the desk, then the office where the desk stood.

ct-freelance.m: Walter Scott's novel Ivanhoe is the first known use, for medieval mercenaries who roamed without a lord.

ct-pen.m: Latin penna means feather, a trace of the quill era. For the same reason, Spanish pluma and German Feder mean both feather and pen.

ct-pencil.m: Pencil comes from Latin penicillus (paintbrush, originally “little tail”). It's unrelated to penna (feather) but related to penicillin.

ct-yeonpil.h: 鉛筆 (pencil) is named for lead but has none
ct-yeonpil.m: The core is graphite, but Europeans once took it for lead and called it black lead. German Bleistift is likewise a “lead stick.”

ct-tegami.h: Japan's 手紙 (letter) is ‘toilet paper’ in China
ct-tegami.m: Same characters, but in Japanese it's a letter and in Chinese it's toilet paper. A letter in Chinese is xìn (信).

ct-news.h: News isn't an acronym for the compass points
ct-news.m: It's a plural meaning “new things.” The compass-point acronym story is folk etymology from a 1640 joke book.

ct-sinmun.h: In Chinese, 新聞 isn't a newspaper but ‘the news’
ct-sinmun.m: Literally “newly heard,” it's a newspaper in Korean (sinmun) and Japanese but the news in Chinese. Chinese for newspaper is bàozhǐ (报纸).

ct-ticket.h: Ticket and etiquette were once the same word
ct-ticket.m: From Old French estiquette, a note you stick up. French étiquette still means both label and etiquette.

ct-map.m: Latin mappa was a cloth like a napkin. A world drawn on cloth, mappa mundi, gave us map, and napkin is a relative.

ct-gift.m: It first meant something given; the leading theory is it became poison as a euphemism for a harmful gift. Mitgift (dowry) keeps the old sense.

ct-chess.h: Chess and check both come from ‘king’
ct-chess.m: Persian shāh (king) passed through Arabic to become eschec, the cry of “check!” Its plural became chess.

ct-ballot.h: A ballot was originally ‘a little ball’
ct-ballot.m: Italian palla (ball) in its small form gave ballot; its big form, pallone, gave balloon. In Venice, people voted with small balls.

ct-balldance.h: The ball you dance at isn't the ball you throw
ct-balldance.m: The round ball is Germanic, but the dance comes from Latin ballare (to dance). Ballet and Spanish bailar are on the dance side.

ct-sajin.m: Meaning “copying the true likeness,” it referred to portraits until 19th-century Japan made it the translation of photograph.

ct-camera.m: Short for camera obscura (dark room), which projected the outside view. Italian camera still means room.
